A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same evolving work on block verification for speculative decoding. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial revisions.

before.justification: V1 reports original block-efficiency and wall-clock experiments across seven datasets and three draft lengths in Section 5 and Appendix C, Tables 2–4.

after.justification: V2 reports original experiments across eight datasets, two drafters, and three draft lengths, including comparisons of token, block, and greedy block verification in Sections 5–6 and Appendices C–D.

M1.justification: V1's verifier uses block probability ratios and modifies target distributions for subsequent tokens; it survives as greedy block verification in v2 Appendix C. V2 introduces a different main verifier with recursively clipped acceptance probabilities and a revised residual distribution, allowing subsequent iterations to use the unchanged target model.

E1.justification: V2 adds GPT Prompt, comprising ChatGPT prompts sourced from LearnGPT, while retaining all seven datasets evaluated in v1. This modestly expands prompt coverage within the existing language-generation evaluation.

E2.justification: Token verification remains the principal baseline. V2 Appendix C, Table 3 adds a three-way comparison by evaluating the earlier proposed procedure, renamed greedy block verification, against the new block verifier and token verification. The additional methods discussed in related work are not experimental baselines.

E3.justification: V2 expands from one reported Gecko/Bison pairing to XXS and XXXS drafters with an S target; the PDFs do not establish how the original names map to these checkpoints. Both retain 1000 prompts, 512-token input limits, 128-token output limits, and draft lengths 4, 6, and 8. Timing tables change from normalized latency to speedup ratios.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's draft-length analysis, v2 investigates the effect of drafter choice and directly compares greedy and non-greedy block verification. Figures 3–4 and Appendix C, Table 3 address whether better drafters amplify gains and whether maximizing acceptance within one block improves iterative decoding.

E5.justification: Both versions report averaging across three random seeds. V2 newly reports standard deviations for efficiencies, speedups, and relative improvements in Table 1 and Tables 4–8. This improves uncertainty reporting without establishing an increase in run count.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive results for the new verifier, GPT Prompt, and the second drafter. Table 3 reports LM1B efficiencies of 3.21 for token, 3.49 for new block, and 3.30 for greedy verification; the last retains v1's 3.299 after rounding. Some baseline values change, while detailed greedy timing and shorter-block results disappear. Changed procedures and unmapped model names limit direct cross-version score comparisons.

T1.justification: V1's single-block optimal-transport result largely survives for greedy verification in v2 Appendix C. V2 adds a validity characterization for the unchanged decoding loop and proofs of distribution preservation and optimal expected token production after any fixed number of iterations for the new verifier (Theorems 1–2, Appendix B).

C1.justification: The central contribution shifts from optimizing acceptance within one block through optimal transport to a verifier with optimal expected token production across iterations in the standard decoding loop. V2 also recommends default adoption and quantifies its headline wall-clock improvement as 5%–8%, while retaining the lossless-generation claim.

C2.justification: V2 explains how greedy acceptance can impair later iterations through target-distribution modifications and why that procedure cannot simply replace verification in the unchanged loop. It explicitly qualifies the new optimality guarantee by this algorithmic scope and adds an interpretation connecting drafter quality to verification gains.

D1.justification: V2 adds NumPy implementation sketches and explicit input-array shapes in Appendix A, plus dataset-source references for GPT Prompt and ShareGPT. These extend v1's pseudocode documentation, although the new implementations are explicitly described as illustrative and unsuitable for practical use.

R1.justification: Section 7 and Table 2 expand the existing taxonomy with TriForce, Online Speculative Decoding, multi-token prediction, and self-speculative or early-exit approaches. V2 also adds stochastic-dominance and dataset references and removes Shazeer 2019. The central positioning of verification improvements as complementary to drafting improvements remains.

P1.justification: The main text is substantially rewritten around a motivating example and a directly usable verifier, replacing the earlier optimal-transport-led narrative. Related work becomes a separate section, experimental setup and results are separated, and the appendices are reorganized around implementation, new proofs, and greedy verification. The title and author list also change.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the decoding diagram, places verification algorithms side by side with highlighted differences, and adds boxed formulas, performance summaries, and implementation figures. The earlier Bernoulli plot is removed. Result tables gain uncertainty and average rows, and new drafter and three-way comparison tables substantially expand the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses the important gap between v1's single-block acceptance objective and performance across decoding iterations. It introduces a verifier that avoids future target-distribution modifications, supplies corresponding theory, and directly compares it with the earlier procedure (Theorem 2; Appendix C, Table 3). Drafter analyses, standard deviations, and clearer algorithm presentation substantially strengthen the paper. Some earlier greedy timing details are omitted and implementation sketches remain limited, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the stronger formulation and supporting evidence.
